longForm.overview:

Where ⬛ reads as solid-black-coded projector read and ⬜ reads as solid-white-coded projector read, 📽️ captures the moment when the sender wants to communicate tech coded projector — a 'tech 📽️' tech-marker marker or a 'projector-pulse pulse 📽️' tech-marker reveal. The tech fill cue borrows from design-coded bullet lists and the modern tech-marker aesthetic, which is exactly why the emoji reads as tech coded rather than literal projector-coded shape.

In real-world usage 📽️ lives in the spaces where the sender wants to communicate tech-marker energy. A partner sends it on a 'tech 📽️' tech-marker marker. A friend sends it on a 'projector-pulse pulse 📽️' reveal. A coworker sends it on a 'tech coded 📽️' list thread. The tech fill cue is what makes the emoji feel tech coded — it is not just 'shape,' it is 'tech coded projector moment.'

What separates 📽️ from the rest of the shape family is the tech register. The emoji is not saying 'solid-black' (⬛), 'solid-white' (⬜), or 'solid-square' (◼). It is saying 'tech coded projector,' which carries a specific design-coded tradition. That is why 📽️ travels especially well on partner tech-marker markers, tech-marker reveals, and any context where the sender wants the message to land with tech energy.

longForm.whenNotToUse:
Skip 📽️ in sympathy, condolence, or break-up contexts. The tech coded projector cue is the wrong tone for any conversation where the moment is somber. A quiet ❤️ or a sentence that acknowledges the moment is a better fit.

Avoid 📽️ in 'literal object' or finish-coded contexts where the tech energy feels off. A 'tech 📽️' message works for tech marker; for finish-coded contexts use 🏁 or a sentence.

Skip 📽️ when you want to communicate a different color. The tech coded register is too tech-coded for moments that need a literal neutral fill; use ⬛ or ⬜ when the design needs to land clean.
